headline: Sept. 7: Washington's Eddy Still Hasn't Let Go
subhead: Late-season warmth is keeping the drop-off lit while the fleet waits on the new moon tide to reset everything inshore.
body_markdown:
By early September most years, Washington is already three months into its run and starting to show the first signs of fatigue — the filament thins, the eddy slides off the edge, and the bite gets patchy waiting on the fall reset. Not this year. The warm water that's been sitting over the canyon since July hasn't broken down, and that's kept the pelagic pattern alive later into the season than it usually runs. This is exactly the kind of stretch where Washington's positional advantage shows up — closer to the Gulf Stream's northern wobble than the canyons above it, so when a filament holds, it holds here first and longest. We flagged this last week, saying to expect continuity with the strong conditions showing up at the neighboring grounds over the next 48 to 72 hours, and that's more or less what's played out. The eddy is still pinned against the drop-off, still pushing bait up onto the edge, and the troll bite hasn't shut off the way it typically does once Labor Day passes.

What's thinner right now is direct word out of the canyon itself. The bulk of the fresh reporting this week has come from inshore — striped bass starting to organize on bunker schools ahead of the new moon, fluke tapering off across the back bays, bluefish showing heavy on the surf. Boats that did make the run to Washington aren't talking much yet, which in September usually means one of two things: either it was quiet enough nobody wants to admit it, or it was good enough they're not ready to share the numbers with the rest of the dock. Given the water's still holding warm and the bait's still stacked on the edge, I'd lean toward the second explanation, but until more boats check in, treat this week as a solid setup rather than a confirmed slam.

The pattern that's been working all summer should still be the play — running the spread along the 100-fathom curve where the wall breaks and the water color changes from green to blue, working the seam where the warm eddy water meets the cooler inshore push. That temperature break is where the bait balls up, and where yellowfin have been sitting all season, mixed with a scattering of bigger bigeye showing at night on the chunk. Ballyhoo skirted with small Ilanders in green-and-yellow and pink-and-white have been the standard producers trolled at 6 to 7 knots, spread wide with a couple of naked ballyhoo tucked closer to the transom for wahoo, which have been the wildcard fish all summer — show up in bunches for a few days, then go quiet for a week. Mahi have been riding shotgun on any floating structure or grass lines along the edge; a few dolphin flags in the 10 to 20 pound class, with the occasional bull mixed in around anything holding sargassum. White marlin numbers have been softer the last couple weeks, which tracks — they tend to thin out earlier than the tuna as the calendar turns toward fall, and that pattern doesn't look to be changing.

For the chunk bite after dark, butterflied bunker and fresh squid strips on circle hooks, fished on a slow drift with the current pushing across the structure, have been the way boats have connected on bigger bigeye and the occasional bluefin mixed through. The key has been staying patient on anchor or drift through the middle of the night rather than moving off structure too early — the bite window out here has been running later than the typical June/July pattern, closer to midnight through the first gray light.

Looking at the next few days, the setup favors continuity if the eddy stays put. The new moon arrives September 10, and that tide swing usually does two things out here: it tightens up the bait on the edge for a day or two before the current gets sloppy, and it can either reinforce the eddy position or start to push it around, depending on how the deeper water shifts underneath it. If the filament holds through the new moon like it's held through everything else this summer, expect the tuna and mahi bite to stay active on the drop-off, with wahoo still a possibility for boats willing to pull a long spread through open water between structure. If the eddy starts to slide — which is the more typical September move — the fish will likely track with it, and boats may need to run a little further off the edge to stay on the same water they're used to fishing closer in.

Best case for this weekend: the warm water stays anchored, the tuna stay stacked tight to the wall, and the fleet gets another clean window before fall conditions start pushing the pattern south and offshore for good. Worst case, the new moon current stirs things up enough that the eddy repositions, and boats spend a day re-locating the temperature break before getting back on fish. Either way, Washington's still playing out ahead of its usual September script, and that's worth taking advantage of while it lasts. If there's only one trip left in the budget this month, this is the window — the water's still doing what it's supposed to do, even if the radio traffic hasn't fully caught up yet.
